Learn how to start automating, as well as how you can start to setup your software factory with governance, monitoring, and security so you can roll out automations to everyone in your business!

title: Agentic engineering past the pilot: An enterprise playbook

He offers a practical perspective on how organizations can move beyond individual productivity gains and scale GitHub Copilot and AI-powered workflows across teams and the software development lifecycle. 

When he's not improving software processes, Phil can be found cooking, biking, skiing down short Midwestern hills, or playing board games.

abstract:
The industry has moved from code completion to chat to agents, and now into AI-native software delivery. But what does that actually look like inside an enterprise, where governance, developer experience, and adoption at scale all have to coexist? 

Through live demos spanning IDE, CLI, and multi-session orchestration, Nick Liffen and Philip Holleran will share the system-level patterns that move agentic engineering from experiment to operating model.

title: Securing MCP: Real exploits, what actually mitigates them, and what doesn't
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

He has helped shape the future of agentic workflows on GitHub, collaborating closely with the open source community and industry pioneers. Outside of tech, Sam is a former professional drummer and enjoys blen

abstract:
There's a running joke that the "S" in MCP stands for security. Funny, but is it fair? MCP is showing up in production and in sensitive environments faster than its security story is settling, and it's worth asking what you're actually exposed to.

This interactive session breaks down MCP security as it really stands today: what the threats are, which layer each one operates on, and how to host MCP servers in production without opening yourself up. You'll look at real exploits and vulnerabilities that have already surfaced, sort the mitigations that hold up from the ones that don't, and dig into where the spec and ecosystem still leave gaps, drawing on what GitHub has learned running this in the real world.

You'll leave with a clear view of MCP's current risks and a practical sense of what's safe to do today, what isn't yet, and what to watch as the ecosystem matures.

title: Shut the context window! You're letting the tokens out

speakers.name: Dylan McCarthy
speakers.title: Principal Solution Consultant
speakers.bio:
Dylan is a Principal Solution Consultant at Versent, working at the intersection of modernization, developer experience, and AI-assisted software development. He helps organizations adopt tools like GitHub Copilot in ways that improve how developers actually work, balancing productivity, cost, and quality.

With a background spanning development, DevOps, and platform engineering, Dylan brings a systems-level perspective to developer workflows, focusing on how tools, context, and teams interact in practice. He is a Microsoft MVP, an active member of the tech community, and regularly speaks abou

abstract:
GitHub Copilot builds context from your open files, related code, and conversation history before every interaction, but most developers never see how much that payload grows. Understanding that mechanism is the difference between sharp output and token bloat. 

In this session, Dylan McCarthy shows how Copilot constructs context in practice, demonstrates the developer habits that quietly inflate token usage, and walks through focused workflows that produce better results with less overhead.  

Dylan will also demo lightweight GitHub-native guardrails that help teams catch overly broad changes before they merge. You'll leave with a mental model of context mechanics and practical patterns you can apply immediately.

title: Your benchmark is lying: What evals actually look like

speakers.bio: Julie is a Product Manager working on Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot, focused on helping developers build with confidence and joy. She has always loved the editor space because it's where small ideas turn into reality: every day, millions of developers open VS Code to explore ideas, debug problems, and ship software. Today, her work centers on LLM releases in VS Code and Copilot Chat, bringing AI capabilities to developers in a practical, high-quality way and improving how they use AI in their daily workflows. She also focuses on offline evaluations for VS Code, building evals to measur

abstract:
Public benchmarks suggest AI coding tools are nearly solved. Developer feedback tells a different story. After a year of shipping models from multiple frontier labs inside GitHub Copilot, the team has learned that the gap between "scores well on SWE-bench" and "developers actually keep using it" is enormous and widening. 

Julia Kasper and Walker Chabbott go behind the scenes on how GitHub Copilot evaluates models in production: what they measure, what they've stopped measuring, the signals that correlate with real developer outcomes, and why your favorite leaderboard may be leading your team astray. You'll leave with a practical framework for building your own eval system (no dedicated research team required).

This session will demonstrate how agents helped CVS Health and UST moved from Jenkins to GitHub Actions by reducing repetitive work and keeping engineers in full control.  

You’ll see how an enterprise put agents to work in a complex migration, and leave with a practical way to plan a CI/CD modernization that addresses legacy complexity today while creating a foundation for future agent-powered development.

title: Stop malicious packages before they reach your build with GitHub Package Firewall
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Eric Sorenson
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: Eric is a product manager at GitHub, focused on supply chain security. He’s been working on open source at scale for a couple of decades, first as an SRE and more recently as a PM. For a thrilling conversation, ask him about Software Bill of Materials data formats, SPDX license expressions, or transitive package dependencies. Outside of tech, Eric does live audio and lighting for heavy metal concerts and enjoys getting muddy on his gravel bike.

abstract:
A wave of recent high-profile attacks has exploited a single weakness: the privileges baked into CI/CD pipelines. An attacker who lands a malicious package in your build can steal the credentials your runner holds, or inject malware that ships to everyone downstream. Securing the build environment has never mattered more.

GitHub Package Firewall sits between your build and upstream package registries, screening dependencies before they ever reach your runner, so a compromised package is blocked at the door instead of executing with your pipeline's privileges. It's a new service and free to use.

In this session, you'll see how the firewall works, how to put it in front of your own builds, and how it protects the users who depend on what you ship.

abstract: The value of an agent isn’t measured by how much code it writes, but by how much software work it finishes. Agents are moving beyond code generation to help plan, review, secure, deploy, and operate software. In this session, GitHub Chief Product Officer Mario Rodriguez explores a new operating model where developers define the outcomes and standards, agents carry work through the development loop, and people remain accountable for what ships. See how GitHub is connecting the context, workflows, and controls teams need to delegate more ambitious work with confidence.

title: I made my Octolamp think with GitHub Copilot CLI hooks

Bea is the first Venezuelan American to have a life-size statue in the Smithsonian. She was recognized as an IF/THEN Ambassador for her work championing women and underrepresented communities in STEM. Born in Venezuela and raised between Venezuela, Miami, and Berlin, she di

abstract:
At Universe 2025, GitHub handed out Octolamps. Beatris Mendez Gandica wondered: what if hers could show when GitHub Copilot CLI is thinking? So she built it.

Using the native hooks system, her lamp breathes green when the agent works, goes white when idle, and blinks red on errors. No prompting tricks, just system-level lifecycle events driving a physical light via the WLED API. 

In this session, Beatris shows what she built, how Copilot CLI hooks work under the hood, and why connecting software to hardware made the concept click. You'll leave knowing how to write your own hooks for any use case. (Pro tip: the repo is open source and works with any WLED device!)

title: Building AI fluency at UPS

Jared also leads the adoption of next-generation tools such as GitHub Copilot, establishing best practices for their secure and effective use.

abstract:
Getting developers to try GitHub Copilot is simple. Getting them fluent with it — using agents to plan, write, and ship real work — is the harder challenge. This session shares how UPS is tackling that, from a developer-focused architect's perspective: how developers move from awareness to fluency, why motivation and measurement matter as much as the tooling, and how faster code generation shifts bottlenecks to new places across the SDLC.

You'll leave with a practical view of what building AI fluency actually takes at enterprise scale, and where to focus first.

title: Four primitives to evaluate and improve your on-call agent's autonomy (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Steven Karis
speakers.title: Chief Architect
speakers.bio: Steven is a founding engineer at ResolveAI. He focuses on building the agentic AI systems that power ResolveAI's Production Engineer. He previously held engineering roles at Splunk and Uber.

abstract: On-call isn't a single kind of work, so treating agent autonomy as one switch (trusted or not) breaks down fast. This session splits on-call into four primitives: triaging alerts, investigating them, acting on production, and learning from what happened. Each progresses at a different rate: investigation is bottlenecked on quality, while action is limited by trust. We'll share how we build frontier agents at Resolve AI, including the shadow diff we use to tell which limit you're actually against, and how to promote and demote autonomy safely, per decision class rather than per agent. You'll leave able to place your own on-call agents against a working reference and know where to focus to improve them.

title: How GitHub taught Copilot to remember and when to forget

speakers.name: Cooper Nederhood
speakers.title: Senior Applied Researcher
speakers.bio: Cooper is a senior software engineer at GitHub on the GitHub Copilot Applied Science Modeling team. His work has focused on building custom Copilot models for enterprise customers. He has also worked to improve Copilot code completion quality through additional LLM fine-tuning and prompt engineering techniques.

speakers.name: Alejandro Carderera
speakers.title: Staff Applied Researcher
speakers.bio:
Alejandro builds AI that developers actually want to use. As a Staff Applied Researcher at GitHub, he works on Copilot—helping AI agents review code more effectively, learn from past sessions, and improve over time at a scale that reaches millions of developers every day. 

Before shipping AI products, Alejandro spent years researching how to make machine learning systems faster and more reliable. He earned a Ph.D. from Georgia Tech, published at leading AI conferences including NeurIPS and ICML, and co-authored a book on large-scale optimization published by SIAM. He later applied that resear

abstract:
Real developer work is sequential, but today's AI agents treat every task as a fresh start. What if Copilot could carry forward what it learned from your last session and drop what no longer applies? 

Alejandro Carderera De Diego and Cooper Nederhood built a benchmark from chains of real GitHub pull requests to test this and found a counterintuitive result: accumulated context can hurt performance.  

That finding powered two features now in development: Skill Forge and Copilot REM. In this session, you'll learn how both work, the measurable improvements they produce, and how to apply these principles to your own agent workflows.

title: Supercharge Copilot code review with custom review instructions

speakers.name: Nish Sinha
speakers.title: Software Engineer III
speakers.bio:
Nish is a software engineer at GitHub, where he has spent his entire five-year career on the Dependabot team. His work sits underneath the dependency updates that flow to millions of repositories. It's the part of Dependabot that nobody sees.

He became interested in software through a combination of the video games he played as a kid, robotics competitions throughout school, and computer science clubs in college. 

Nish lives in Atlanta, where he enjoys his coffee, code, and cars.

abstract:
GitHub's Dependabot team added custom Copilot code review instructions to their 10-year-old backend repository, and the results showed up fast: review time dropped, comment volume dropped, and Copilot now automatically catches real, domain-specific bugs that used to require a human reviewer to spot.

The key was where the instructions came from. Instead of writing review rules from scratch, the team used Copilot to mine their own PR review history for the patterns their reviewers flag again and again, then turned those recurring patterns into custom instruction files. The result is a reviewer that already knows the conventions, pitfalls, and domain quirks of a decade-old codebase.

This session walks through exactly how they did it, and how you can run the same workflow on your own repository.

title: Real ways we cut token costs without slowing developers

speakers.name: Vicky Israni
speakers.title: Senior Solutions Engineer
speakers.bio:
Vicky is a Solutions Engineer at GitHub with extensive experience in software development, specializing in backend development and low-latency programming. His background spans cybersecurity, industrial automation, and avionics. 

Passionate about driving innovation in DevOps, automation, and cybersecurity, Vicky partners with companies to tackle their DevSecOps challenges head-on.

abstract:
AI coding tools can boost productivity, but they can also increase costs. Token-based pricing changes how teams think about performance, efficiency, and even code quality. But many don’t see where tokens are being wasted until it hurts.  

This session will show you real examples of token waste — bloated prompts, repeated context, noisy CI workflows — along with practical changes you can implement to reduce consumption without slowing down developers. You’ll also learn how to identify common sources of waste, optimize token usage, and scale AI-assisted development more efficiently.

title: Four days, zero lines: The AI force multiplier

Jeff is a recognized leader and active voice in the engineering community, having served as a host on Software Engineering Radio and appearing on shows such as The Engineering Career Coach. When he isn’t using GitHub Copilot as a force multiplie

abstract:
How do you clear a massive governance backlog without destroying developer velocity? In just four days, Jeff Doolittle of Trimble used GitHub Copilot to build an automated system and rapidly clear the backlog without manually writing a single line of code. In this session, you’ll learn how to use AI not just as a coding assistant, but as an architectural force multiplier.  

You'll leave knowing how to combine automated GitHub Actions with custom Copilot prompts. This combination will give you the tools to eliminate developer toil, easily enforce remediation lifecycles, empower others to adopt AI tools, and make the "right path" the easiest path for your entire engineering org.

abstract: How should developers use local and cloud intelligence together? GitHub and Windows show how Copilot's intelligent orchestration can bring local models into the Copilot workflow. GitHub provides the developer experience and orchestration; Windows provides the hardware, runtime, and optimized environment for on-device inference. This session will explore how Auto mode can help match work to the right compute environment while keeping local and cloud intelligence complementary.

abstract: As AI agents produce more code, teams need to know what those agents bring into a build and how to verify what ships. This demo shows how JFrog works with GitHub to control which models, MCP servers, and packages agents use; replace supported vulnerable dependencies with patched versions when available; and enforce compliance policies using signed evidence. You’ll see where those controls fit in the development workflow and what teams can review when auditing a release.

title: Beyond correct: Making code quality worth acting on

speakers.name: James Fletcher
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: James works on GitHub Advanced Security and primarily focuses on helping security-conscious users find and fix more security problems in their code.

speakers.name: Caro Galvin
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: As a Senior Product Manager with a rich background in product, software development, and test development, Caro is a collaborative problem solver who thrives working on complex technical products. Currently working at GitHub as senior product manager for code scanning, she brings a decade of experience in cross-functional teams to untangle complex processes and create seamless workflows. Outside work, she builds production automation for community theatre volunteers, because every domain has a workflow worth improving.

abstract:
When AI generates more code, static analysis surfaces more findings. More findings should mean better code. Instead, it usually means more noise nobody acts on.

Over the past year, the team measured that problem across 165,000+ pull requests and 100K+ repositories. The data was pointed: 54% of PRs with findings have the same rule firing over and over, and developers dismiss quality findings at nearly the same rate as security findings while perceiving them as far noisier.

This session turns that research into practical guidance: why "more findings" backfires, the design philosophy that finally moved adoption, and specific decisions traced back to the data, like grouping repeated findings into one comment and surfacing fixes inline instead of in a dashboard nobody opened. Expect live demos and real before-and-after PR examples. You'll leave knowing how to make automated feedback something developers actually trust and act on.

title: The Low Orbit Agentic Cannon: Scaling Copilot through internal tooling

speakers.name: Callum Cieciala
speakers.title: VP, Developer Experience
speakers.bio:

He oversees the company’s GitHub footprint across more than 15 organizations and 1,200 repositories. Over the past year, he has gone from cautiously assigning two-point Jira tickets to AI agents to launching hundreds of autonomous pull requests across the organization in a single morning, while building the production tools that made it possible. 

As VP of Developer Experience, Callum is part of the team responsible for CI/CD, GitHub governance, and developer tooling across Galaxy’s

abstract:
In December 2025, more than 300 autonomous pull requests were opened in a single morning — each written by an AI agent. By March 2026, the same approach generated more than 3,500 architecture documentation files across the organization. This resulted in a 97% success rate, driven by one engineer.  

This session shares how the Galaxy team internally developed the tools behind this effort: from Air Traffic Controller, which routed Jira tickets to Copilot cloud agents, to the Low Orbit Agentic Cannon, which scaled work across hundreds of repositories.  

You'll learn what worked, what stalled, and the lessons gained from operating agentic systems at scale, along with why proven engineering fundamentals mattered more than the AI itself.

title: Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills

speakers.name: Andrea Griffiths
speakers.title: Senior Developer Advocate

She ships skills, not software, and most of it happens from her phone.

speakers.name: Shishir Tewari
speakers.title: Senior Manager, Data Engineering
speakers.bio: Shishir Tewari is Head of Enterprise Data Engineering at Procore Technologies, where he leads strategic architecture for Marketing, Finance, and Advanced Analytics using AI/ML. He brings over two decades of experience building data platforms at scale, including previous engineering leadership roles at Google and Amazon.

abstract:
Most developers use AI the same way: open a chat, type a prompt, move on. The context disappears. The next step starts from scratch. Skills break that cycle: reusable files that capture how you want an agent to work. Andrea Griffiths builds them for her own recurring work: files any coding agent can run. Shishir Tewari builds them for a data engineering team at Procore, where a skill has to encode senior-engineer judgment and survive production. Different scale, same format. The file you write for yourself tonight is the same file that runs a team's pipeline.

After this session, you'll have a clear model for when to build a skill instead of writing another prompt.

A factory isn't defined by what it produces. It's defined by the process that produces it. The GitHub Agentic Workflows team built one: five engineers, GitHub Actions as the floor, agents as the crew, 460 pull requests a week. Peli de Halleux from the GitHub Next team shows you how it's wired. Marks & Spencer shows how it scales: from a proof-of-concept that raised 123 issues and fixed 77 the same day, to a central control plane deploying governed workflows across the organization. Provation brings the regulated perspective: what it looks like to adopt agentic development in healthcare, where every automated decision needs an audit trail, and how it can strengthen an already mature compliance program.

You'll leave knowing how an agentic development factory comes together, what it takes to run one, and how teams across retail, healthcare, and beyond are putting it to work today.

abstract: You and your agent just built something that works on your laptop. Grant Griffiths shows what it takes to wire two AI agents together via MCP, what the handoff object actually looks like, and where it breaks down in practice. You'll leave with a concrete architecture for multi-agent incident resolution and a realistic picture of what works today.

title: The O(1) patch: Securing the supply chain against AI-discovered zero-days
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Ron Efroni
speakers.title: CEO and Co-Founder
speakers.bio:
Ron is the CEO and co-founder of Flox and President of the NixOS Foundation, bringing Nix to the world with over 10,000 contributors.

Ron started his career as a software engineer before going on to lead the development of large-scale field-operated products. A repeat founder, Ron moved into developer tooling at Meta’s Facebook as head of developer products, building the tools powering Meta’s 20,000-strong developer core. Recognizing the limitations of existing tooling and the power of Nix, Ron co-founded Flox to make Nix more accessible to the wider engineering community.

abstract:
AI models can now autonomously discover decades-old CVEs, which means the software supply chain has never been more fragile. When the next zero-day drops, scanning your infrastructure node-by-node with non-deterministic package managers is an O(n) problem: by the time you know where you're exposed, you're already too late.

This session explores a different foundation. By shifting to deterministic package management — built on the principles of NixOS and nixpkgs — CVE detection and remediation become an O(1) lookup against a fixed, cryptographic manifest of exactly what's in your system. Instead of asking "are we affected?" and scanning to find out, you already know, instantly and provably.

You'll leave understanding what "secure by construction" really means, how deterministic builds change your exposure model when a zero-day hits, and what it takes to move toward this approach in a real supply chain.

title: Auth for agents: How auth.md lets agents skip the sign-up form (Sponsored)

abstract:
Every AI agent hits the same wall: to act on a user's behalf, someone still has to create an account, generate an API key, and paste it into a config file. auth.md is WorkOS's open protocol for skipping that step. Services publish a lightweight auth.md file pointing agents to a standard discovery document. From there, an agent that already knows who its user is can exchange that identity for scoped, short-lived credentials to your API. No signup form, no copied API key, no separate developer console.

In this live demo, WorkOS will show auth.md end-to-end: an agent discovering support for the protocol, asserting a user's identity, and getting back scoped credentials it can use immediately — plus what it takes to add auth.md support to your own API.

You'll leave understanding how the protocol works under the hood, why identity-based credential exchange is safer than long-lived API keys, and how to publish your own auth.md file so any agent can authenticate to your API without a single copied secret.

title: Bringing AI-detected secret scanning to push time and on-prem environments
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

abstract:
Secret detection has a four-body problem: confidence, speed, performance under load, and cost. Pattern matching is fast and cheap, but it misses the long tail of credentials without recognizable formats. Hosted LLMs catch more, but they aren’t built for the critical path of every push — where every decision has a sub-second latency budget — or for air-gapped GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) environments, where the model has to run on-premises instead of calling out to a hosted LLM.

In this demo, you’ll see GitHub’s AI-powered secret scanning bring secrets to two new surfaces: push protection, where unstructured credentials are blocked before they land in a repository, and GHES, where the same detection runs fully on-premises with no hosted LLM required.

You’ll leave knowing how GitHub detects secrets at push time and on-premises: intelligent enough to catch what pattern matching misses, fast enough to run on every push, and portable enough for air-gapped GHES.

That's how confidence becomes trust, and you'll leave knowing how to build a loop where speed and accuracy work as one.

He brings more than 16 years of experience in software strategy, cloud architecture, information security, and digital transformation, including former CTO and Chief Digital Officer roles. He also teaches at the university level and advises organizations on building governed, production-ready AI engineering practices.

speakers.title: Tech Lead Venture
speakers.bio:
Leonardo Villa Rodriguez is a Tech Lead and Venture Architect based in Medellín, Colombia, who specializes in taking ideas from concept to launch. 

At itti, he develops new business ventures and uses AI and automation to optimize the product lifecycle. Drawing on his experience leading digital transformation in the financial sector, Leonardo focuses on improving returns on investment and scaling platforms efficiently. He believes the future of product management lies in orchestrating AI agents to amplify human capabilities. 

When he's not redefining how fast regulated software can ship, Leon

abstract:
Ueno Ads, an in-app advertising product for the UENO banking platform, was scoped as a six-month build with a full delivery squad: product, engineering leadership, UX, developers, and QA. The team at itti shipped it in four weeks, with one product manager directing agents on GitHub. 

Inside a regulated bank, that only holds up if a person can approve and trace every step. Javier Durán and Leonardo Esteban Villa show the pipeline itti built to make that true, the gates that got it through cybersecurity review, and where the bottleneck moved once agents were doing the writing. You'll leave knowing where humans need to stay in the loop and what it takes for agent-written work to survive a security review.

title: Who's watching the agents? What AI code does in production
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Donia Chaiehloudj
speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer
speakers.bio:
Donia Chaiehloudj is a Software Engineer at Isovalent and a member of the technical community advocacy team, where she focuses on open source, developer education, and sharing practical knowledge through talks, workshops, and technical content. She contributes to the Cilium project, working at the intersection of Kubernetes, Linux networking, and eBPF to improve how distributed systems are secured and observed at runtime. 

Donia is the co-author of Learn Go with Pocket-Sized Projects and has a strong interest in building developer tooling in Go, particularly in networking and observability. H

abstract:
GitHub Copilot and coding agents can now write, commit, and deploy code autonomously, and GitHub gives you a powerful control plane over how that software is created and shipped. But once the code runs in production, its behavior gets much harder to see. Static analysis and PR review can inspect code at rest; neither can observe a running process.

This session shows how eBPF-based runtime observability extends that model down into the kernel, giving you visibility into the processes, file access, and network activity of AI-generated workloads as they actually execute. When an agent's code reaches out to an unexpected endpoint or touches a file it shouldn't, you see it.

You'll leave with a practical way to close the security loop that AI introduces: not just reviewing what agents write, but watching what their code actually does once it's live.

title: Turning user feedback into requirements with a custom Copilot agent

She is also an affiliate faculty member at the University of Washington, where she has spent more than a decade teaching and researching how to design collaborative systems with diverse stakeholders, including public health professionals, first responders, and patients with limited English proficiency. 

Her work has been recognized with awards from the University of Washington College of Engineering and the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). She never grew out of her horse “phase” a

abstract: AI-assisted tools make it easier than ever for more people to turn ideas into working software. But while the barrier to building is falling, the need to evaluate ideas and validate assumptions in order to build the right experience remains. This GitHub App demo shows how an agent can connect feedback signals across multiple channels, creating a unified view of customer needs that helps teams prioritize opportunities, shape requirements, and make more informed product decisions.

title: Going beyond suggestions: How to govern agentic workflows in GitHub (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Parker Johnston
speakers.title: Agentic Field CTO
speakers.bio: Parker Johnston leads Insight’s efforts to build an agentic, AI-driven software development lifecycle. He integrates automation, intelligent coding assistance, and data insights across the development process, helping teams reduce bottlenecks and build software faster and more securely while maintaining quality and compliance.

speakers.name: Dave Benedic
speakers.title: Sr. Manager - Agentic Platforms
speakers.bio: Dave Benedic is an architect on Insight’s National Cloud Enablement & DevOps team, where he helps companies of all sizes navigate cloud transformation. Since entering the IT industry in 2004, he has held roles across development and operations, experience that drives his enthusiasm for DevOps and organizational transformation. Dave brings creativity to his work and enjoys sharing knowledge through mentoring and teaching.

abstract:
Not every engineering task arrives with a clear set of steps. GitHub Agentic Workflows can interpret the situation, decide what to do next, and take action, extending automation to work that usually starts with human triage. That flexibility creates a new challenge: how do teams give agents room to help while keeping permissions, security, and review under human control? 

This session explains the guardrails that make agent-powered workflows manageable, including scoped permissions, workflow governance, safe execution patterns, and review of agent contributions. Through architecture diagrams and workflow examples, you’ll see how teams can use agents to analyze code, maintain repositories, and handle repetitive work without giving them unrestricted access. 

You’ll leave with a practical framework for deciding what an agent can do, what it needs a person to approve, and how to keep its actions secure and auditable.

title: Keep vulnerabilities out of your codebase, without leaving where you build

speakers.name: James Fletcher
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: James works on GitHub Advanced Security and primarily focuses on helping security-conscious users find and fix more security problems in their code.

abstract: A green CI run and a merged pull request don’t tell you whether a change works under real traffic. In this live demo, you’ll see Bluebox by Dynatrace use OpenTelemetry data to brief a coding agent on a microservice app. When the app breaks, the agent opens a pull request with an evidence-backed diagnosis and proposed fix. After review and deployment, the team checks error rates and SLOs for regressions. You’ll leave with a practical model for verifying agent-written changes and deciding where human review, escalation, and a kill switch belong.

title: How to shift specifications from contracts to hypotheses

speakers.name: Julio Arruda
speakers.title: Chief Architect
speakers.bio: Julio is the first Brazilian GitHub Star and has been a Microsoft MVP for 10 years. He is the Chief Architect and GenAI Lead at Wynxx and GFT, and he is also a YouTuber and speaker.

abstract:
Teams building agents and workflows powered by GitHub Copilot are inheriting a habit that quietly breaks: writing specifications as contracts. A traditional spec is binding. But AI doesn't work that way. The same prompt produces different outputs across runs, models, and updates. If you over-trust the spec, you risk shipping features that "passed" while doing the wrong thing. Abandon specs entirely, and you lose control. 

In this session, Julio Arruda walks through two real production failures caused by this pattern, then introduces a working reframe. You'll leave with a three-practice checklist you can apply Monday.

title: How to think about reachability and use it to prioritize vulnerabilities
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

With a unique background that combines data science and software engineering experience, she brings technical depth and user empathy to vulnerability management. In her role, Carlin leads efforts to make security integrate seamlessly into developer workflows, helping organizations prioritize what matters most. Outside of work, she is a board member of her alma mater, Rice University (go Owls!), and a member of the ThinkCyber Foundation. She also enjoys running and plays board games competitively.

speakers.name: Ankit Kumar Honey
speakers.title: Senior Engineering Manager
speakers.bio: Ankit doesn't just manage engineering teams; he safeguards the foundational layers of the global software supply chain. As the Senior Engineering Manager for Dependabot at GitHub, Ankit oversees the automated security of 30 million+ repositories across 35+ ecosystems, turning the tide against supply chain vulnerabilities through the pioneering use of AI coding agents for autonomous remediation. His credibility is rooted in the high-stakes reality of modern infrastructure, where his team's work secures the codebases of sovereign entities including NASA, CISA, and the UK Government. Before stepp

abstract:
Vulnerability prioritization is hard. Severity tells you how serious a flaw is, the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) indicates how likely it is to be exploited, and runtime context shows what's actually running. Reachability adds application-specific context by showing whether your code can call the vulnerable function.
In this session, you'll learn how to use reachability to make more informed prioritization decisions. A live demo will show function-level reachability directly in Dependabot, including the evidence behind the result and how teams may use that information when prioritizing alerts. You'll leave with a practical framework for focusing remediation efforts where they matter most.

title: Beyond the prompt: Building an AI that takes initiative

speakers.name: Cameron Hamilton
speakers.title: Creator
speakers.bio:
Cameron Hamilton is an AI engineer, researcher, and founder of Alliance AI, with more than a decade of experience building applied AI systems. He created HALIE, a proactive AI assistant designed to anticipate users’ needs and help address them. His projects also include Endgame, an open-source machine learning library; the Parkinson’s Insight Engine (PIE); and Alliance Desk, an AI front-desk agent that helps businesses avoid missed bookings.

Cameron’s work explores how AI agents can become more capable and useful while keeping people meaningfully in control. As a public figure and content cre

abstract: Cameron Hamilton asked his AI assistant, HALIE, to connect the camera in his son's nursery. It turned that camera into a baby monitor he never asked for. When he asked it to automate business growth, it told him to meet customers in person. And when he audited its work, 38 of its 96 goals were about improving itself. How do you make a proactive agent dependable? This session walks through HALIE's three systems: anticipation (acting on needs without a prompt), self-evolution (improving its own tools and code), and metacognition (reviewing work and conversations to steer what comes next). Cameron covers experiments in making useful initiative repeatable, the architecture behind it, what it costs to run an agent on cheap models, and which decisions still need a human. You'll leave with practical ways to design agents that decide what to do next, learn from what helped, and earn more responsibility through measurable results.

title: Rediscover the command line: Practical workflows with GitHub CLI

Beyond GitHub, Ryan is the longtime owner and lead developer of one of the world's largest Minecraft theme park recreation servers, where he leads 150+ volunteer staff and has welcomed over 450,000 unique players. An avid theme park fan, Ryan can often be found traveling to — or ot

speakers.name: Ayman Bagabas

Before joining GitHub, he led the open-source Bubble Tea framework at Charmbracelet, which now powers tens of thousands of terminal applications. His code ships in projects ranging from Debian Linux to the Linux kernel. Outside of work, Ayman makes music and enjoys the outdoors.

abstract:
Are you using the command line to its full potential? In this session, Ryan Hecht and Ayman Bagabas start with fundamentals like Unix pipes and shell scripts, and builds up to real workflows using GitHub CLI, Git, Gum, and GitHub Copilot CLI.  

Showing how each tool connects into workflows you can take back to your terminal immediately, this demo is full of real scripts solving real problems. You'll leave with a stronger command line foundation and concrete workflows that make you faster, whether you're a CLI skeptic or already live in the terminal.

title: GitHub Copilot at scale: An interactive lab for enterprise admins

speakers.name: David Losert

He helps customers define their technology strategies and achieve better outcomes using GitHub as an agent-native DevSecOps platform. David is skilled at simplifying complex topics and turning ambitious challenges into practical, achievable steps. He also contributes to internal enablement and thought leadership at GitHub. Outside of technology, David is a passionate pizza baker who enjoys making authentic Neapolitan pi

speakers.name: April Yoho
speakers.title: Senior Developer Advocate
speakers.bio: April is a Senior Developer Advocate and DevOps Practice Lead at GitHub, specializing in application transformation and modern DevOps practices. She helps customers move from legacy technology to serverless and container-based development while adopting workflows that put code first. Outside of work, April enjoys hiking, skiing, and scuba diving. She also competes in Ironman and Half Ironman triathlons.

abstract:
Rolling out GitHub Copilot across an enterprise takes more than assigning seats. In this interactive lab run by technical staff, you’ll configure a sample rollout and work through the settings that shape how teams use Copilot. 

We’ll explore utilization-based billing tools, API options, common configuration issues, and the decisions that matter when moving from a pilot to a wider rollout. Bring your questions and leave with a better understanding of Copilot’s enterprise controls, plus a checklist you can adapt to your organization.

title: How to see what your agent is building before it builds it (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Jake Albaugh
speakers.title: Developer Advocate
speakers.bio:
Jake is a Developer Advocate at Figma, where they work across marketing, product, and sales to create value for developers. Before joining Figma, Jake spent 12 years as a software engineer, working across the web stack and helping bridge the gap between design and development. Their experience includes building tools for front-end developers as an early hire at CodePen. 

Creatively, Jake builds web toys at www.jake.fun, teaches algorithmic music and the Web Audio API, and has been playing survival Minecraft since 2010.

abstract:
Your agent is shipping code faster than your team can follow. But there's one problem: nobody can see what's being built before it happens. 

In this session, Jake Albaugh demos a workflow that connects Figma and GitHub Copilot through MCP, showing you how to turn your codebase into a visual plan on a FigJam canvas, get team alignment, and feed that context directly into the GitHub Copilot cloud agent.  

You'll see the full loop live and leave with a repeatable workflow that plugs into your existing GitHub and Figma setup.

title: PATs, rulesets, and IP allowlists: How Confluent secured GitHub Enterprise Cloud
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Luke Young
speakers.title: Principal Security Engineer
speakers.bio:
Luke Young is a Principal Security Engineer at Confluent, where he focuses on GitHub security, CI/CD security, and cloud security. He has presented at DEF CON 23, 24, and 25, and has researched a variety of widely used products and network protocols, resulting in more than 50 CVE assignments. 

Previously, Luke was a Sr. Staff Security Engineer at LinkedIn, where he worked on the company's initial migration to GitHub and helped drive the adoption of CodeQL across LinkedIn's repositories.

abstract: Securing a GitHub Enterprise organization can be an intimidating exercise, especially at scale. In this session, Confluent shares hard-won lessons from rolling out security controls across their organization: what worked, what backfired, and the gaps they didn't see coming. They'll start with the basics, then get into the messy details: managing repos with infrastructure as code, choosing between branch protection and rulesets, migrating from personal access tokens (PATs) to GitHub Apps, rolling out IP allowlists, and more. You'll leave with a practical roadmap for maturing your own GitHub organization's security posture, and a clearer sense of which controls are worth the effort.

speakers.bio:
Angie is the VP of Developer Experience at the Agentic AI Foundation, where she guides how agentic systems are designed, implemented, and adopted across the global developer ecosystem.

As a Master Inventor, Angie is recognized for her innovative, out-of-the-box thinking, which has led to 27 patented inventions in virtual worlds, collaboration software, social networking, smarter planet initiatives, and software development processes.

Priya is a software engineer navigating the intersection of code, community, and collaboration. Most of her work lives in Django and Python, building backend systems and the infrastructure around them, with AWS and CircleCI handling the operational choreography. She cares about code that is explicit about its assumptions, automations that are sensible rather than just clever, clear trust boundaries, and deployments that don’t require theatrics.

On the community side, she is a Django Software Foundation Board Director, serving in the Secretary officer role and helping govern one of the most wi

abstract:
Open source isn't dying. It's being stress-tested in ways nobody anticipated. AI has accelerated contributions and made it easier than ever to ship code, but it's also introduced new questions about quality, governance, and what community means when bots can contribute at machine scale. 

In this session, three leaders from the open source foundations community share what they're actually seeing: why AI makes open source more essential than ever, what maintainers are doing right now to handle the surge in AI-assisted contributions, and how foundations are updating governance structures that were built for human contributors. You'll leave with a clear picture of where open source stands today and what needs to change.

title: Stop guessing: What 100M pull requests and 150T tokens tell us about AI impact (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Adam Ferrari
speakers.title: SVP of Engineering
speakers.bio: Adam is SVP of Engineering at Jellyfish, where he leads the technology strategy that helps engineering organizations measure and maximize the impact of AI-powered development tools, including GitHub Copilot. With more than two decades of experience scaling world-class engineering teams (including as CTO of Endeca through its $1 billion acquisition by Oracle, and at Salsify, where he helped grow the business to over $150 million in ARR), Adam brings a rare combination of deep technical craft and executive leadership. His relationship with Jellyfish runs deep: he was a customer and strategic adv

abstract:
A year ago, the question was: Is GitHub Copilot working? Now there are answers. Jellyfish's analysis of 100+ million pull requests, 90+ million prompts, and 150+ trillion tokens from more than 275K software engineers reveals what high-performing teams do differently with AI coding—and why so many companies still struggle to scale its value.

Adam Ferrari, SVP of Engineering at Jellyfish, shares the data and shows how to separate broad-but-shallow adoption from the patterns that actually move productivity, throughput, and team effectiveness. You'll leave knowing which signals to watch, what distinguishes mature AI programs from surface-level rollouts, and how to connect Copilot activity to metrics your business cares about.

title: What happens between pressing Enter and getting a response from GitHub Copilot

speakers.name: Ken Muse
speakers.title: Staff DevOps Architect | ODST | FDE
speakers.bio: Ken is a Staff DevOps Architect on the ODST team at GitHub. He is a four-time Microsoft Azure MVP (retired) and a Microsoft Certified Trainer, and he was both an ALM | DevOps Ranger and a member of the Microsoft Azure Advisors. Ken is a frequent community speaker and has appeared at GitHub Universe, VSLive!, Live! 360, DevOps World, SQLSaturday, All Day DevOps, Global Azure, and TAG DevOps panels. When not speaking or coding, Ken enjoys playing multiple instruments and composing.

speakers.name: Mickey Gousset
speakers.title: Staff DevOps Architect | ODST | FDE
speakers.bio: Mickey is a staff DevOps architect at GitHub. He is passionate about DevOps and helping developers achieve their goals. Mickey speaks on topics at various user groups, code camps, and conferences around the world.

abstract:
What are AI credits, and why does typing a few words consume thousands of them? Every GitHub Copilot interaction assembles a layered prompt before anything reaches the model. Most developers never see this process, which makes slow or irrelevant responses hard to diagnose. 

In this session, Ken Muse and Mickey Gousset open up the pipeline: how VS Code builds these prompts, how the prioritization engine decides what stays in the context window and what gets silently dropped, and what real-world patterns look like in the debug logs. You'll leave knowing how to engineer your interactions for maximum signal and minimum waste.

title: Building Copilot in the cloud

speakers.name: Jason Etcovitch
speakers.title: Principal Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Jason is a principal software engineer at GitHub, leading the technical teams behind Copilot products. He has a long history of building cool things at GitHub and is now focused on the future of agentic development. When he isn’t pushing AI-assisted development forward, he’s almost certainly showing off cat photos.

abstract: Copilot is great at helping developers write code on their machines, but running agents in the cloud is a major step up in productivity. Making that work takes an experience developers can trust, backed by a safe place to run, the right access to repositories and tools, and enough compute to get the job done. This session goes behind the scenes at how product and platform come together to make cloud agents work, from delegation and review to isolated sandboxes, orchestration, identity, and permissions. You'll leave understanding what it takes to run cloud agents safely, and why you can trust these agents to handle the real work.

title: Agentic modernization of .NET and Java apps with GitHub Copilot

speakers.name: Kaush Ganguly
speakers.title: Sr. Cloud Solution Architect - AI Apps
speakers.bio: Kaush is a Senior Cloud Solution Architect at Microsoft who helps organizations move from experimenting with GitHub Copilot to scaling AI-assisted development securely and responsibly. He leads application modernization and migration initiatives across Australia and New Zealand, working with digital-native and enterprise teams on complex codebases using GitHub Copilot, GitHub Actions, GitHub Advanced Security, Azure AI, and cloud-native delivery patterns. With a background in developer advocacy, Kaush has delivered more than 50 talks, workshops, and hands-on labs for developers, architects, se

abstract:
Legacy app modernization shouldn't start with a blank repo and a risky rewrite. This session shows how GitHub Copilot app modernization — GitHub's AI-powered toolset for upgrading and migrating legacy applications — helps teams analyze, plan, refactor, test, secure, and migrate .NET and Java apps across IDE and CLI workflows.

You'll see a practical modernization playbook that combines GitHub Copilot app modernization, GitHub Actions, built-in security checks, and Azure-ready migration patterns. This turns a traditionally slow, high-risk effort into one that's safer, faster, and repeatable at scale. Rather than rewriting from scratch, teams assess what they have, upgrade frameworks and dependencies, remediate vulnerabilities, validate with tests, and move to the cloud with a human in the loop at each step.

title: From x86/x64 to Arm: Migrating a Large-Scale Linux Web App with GitHub Copilot (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Michael Gamble
speakers.title: partner marketing
speakers.bio: Michael is an AI builder, product leader, and software engineer building products from concept to revenue scale. He has launched and scaled SaaS and AI offerings and led AI platform development through acquisition. His work spans product strategy, ecosystem partnerships, and go-to-market execution, with a practical focus on turning emerging developer workflows into real adoption.

abstract: As software development becomes increasingly agentic, the infrastructure those agents run on matters. In this session, you’ll see GitHub Copilot use the Arm MCP server and multiple Cobalt 200 cloud VMs as Arm-native secondary compute for a real migration workflow: moving an existing x86/x64 Linux web application onto a 100% Arm-native path – from development and builds through GitHub Actions and deployment. Once the app is running, we'll use Arm Performix to pinpoint and fix performance bottlenecks, then validate each optimization with data from the live workload. You’ll leave with three ways to judge the workflow – task success, task time, and cost per successful task – and a clearer sense of how Arm native compute and continuous performance validation fit into agentic development.

title: What Copilot code review catches (and how to build a custom agent for the rest)

David Pereira is a student at heart who is passionate about software development. His experience is primarily in e-commerce, with a focus on event-driven architectures and microservices built using .NET and Azure. 

David has spoken at events and conferences including Cloud Native Lisbon, Java User Group, Azure and AI User Group Portugal, and Global Azure Portugal 2025. Previously, he served on the AsyncAPI Technical Steering Committee and was an active contributor to open source software. David loves learning and sharing his knowledge. 

Outside of work, David enjoys listening to music and re

abstract:
Teams are merging more pull requests per day, and senior engineers can't review them all. 

In this session, David Pereira does a live walkthrough of what Copilot code review handles out of the box, then builds a custom agent using the Copilot SDK with focused sub-agents for concerns like performance and architecture. You'll learn how to pair built-in review with custom agents that enforce your team's specific standards, along with practical patterns for building reliable agents with the SDK.

title: Build without breaking trust (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Aaron Reich
speakers.title: Chief Technology Officer
speakers.bio:
Aaron Reich is Chief Technology Officer at Avanade, where he leads research and development, AI products, and the company’s internal AI transformation. He also practices the fine art of nudging innovation into every corner of the business. His love of technology began when he was young, with his family’s Apple IIC and too many after-school hours in the computer lab. 

Aaron has a soft spot for startups and spends time coaching and mentoring entrepreneurs. He previously served as board president of The Healing Center in Seattle and was a devoted road runner until the arrival of his twin boys ch

abstract:
AI can help a business team get to a working solution quickly. The more challenging test is whether that solution fits into the rest of the stack. In an Avanade project for a manufacturing customer, Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs) rebuilt a business process with the team and proved the technology worked. But the build was designed around that one process, without accounting for core systems, adjacent workflows, or the handoffs between them—so it didn't scale. 

In this session, you’ll see an anonymized before-and-after architecture diagram showing how the team changed its approach by pairing FDEs with a Trust Architect. You’ll learn why a successful proof of concept can still be hard to integrate, what each role owns, and how to assign ownership where low-code work hands off to pro-code engineering.

title: How a shared AI config became Slack's internal tool platform

speakers.name: Frances Coronel
speakers.title: Senior Software Engineer
speakers.bio:
Frances Coronel builds the AI tooling infrastructure that hundreds of engineers at Slack rely on every day. As a Senior Software Engineer on Slack’s Developer Experience team, she created the company’s internal AI tool catalog, adoption metrics dashboard, and cross-functional enablement program, scaling a personal side project into an organization-wide platform in four months. 

Before joining DevXP, Frances spent years as a product engineer shipping features used by millions of Slack users, including leading the Notifications 2.0 redesign that drove a 5x increase in user engagement. She has s

abstract:
Frances Coronel, a product engineer at Slack, built a personal AI setup to work faster and shared it in a public channel. Engineers across the company started forking it without being asked. That organic pull grew into Slack's internal AI tool catalog: a single source of truth for MCP servers, skills, and agents, backed by an adoption dashboard tracking real usage data across teams. 

In this session, Frances demos the catalog, shares six months of real adoption metrics, and shows how a personal productivity hack became org-wide infrastructure. You'll learn how to build an internal AI tool catalog on GitHub, measure adoption with real data instead of surveys, and create the cultural conditions that make AI tooling spread on its own.

title: One skill, one CLI, one production health report

speakers.name: Xin Wu
speakers.title: Principal Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Xin Wu has spent the past 15 years working in databases. She’s currently a Principal Software Engineer at GitHub, where she leads the database teams that keep the data behind GitHub.com running smoothly. Previously, she was at Booking.com as the tech lead for the DB teams. She’s spoken at various conferences, such as Percona Live and Grace Hopper. Lately, she’s been having a lot of fun figuring out how to make AI agents actually useful for production work. Xin lives in Hawaii with her family, plays games whenever she can, and is always up for trying something new.

abstract:
It started as an idea: could Copilot CLI generate a real health report for a database fleet? Xin Wu wrote a single skill, hit a wall, and spent weeks working with the agent until it provided a trustworthy report.  

In this Ship & Tell, Xin shares the journey from first skill to a report accurate enough to actually ship, including how to review AI-generated output without redoing all the work.

title: When is local Copilot worth it? Three open-weight coders vs. Copilot out of the box

speakers.name: Alpha Romer Coma
speakers.title: Senior Data Engineer
speakers.bio:
Alpha Romer Coma is a Senior Data Engineer at ViableView and an independent machine learning engineer specializing in multimodal AI and accelerated computing across text, video, and audio. He has benchmarked more than 20 datacenter, consumer, and edge AI accelerators across training and inference.

At PyTorch Conference Europe 2026, Alpha presented a comparison of PyTorch workloads across NVIDIA H100 GPUs, Google TPUs, and AWS Trainium, covering performance and development tradeoffs.

He is a Google Cloud Certified Professional Machine Learning Engineer, an AWS Certified Machine Learning Engin

abstract:
Bring your own key (BYOK) for GitHub Copilot is now generally available, and open-weight coding models keep landing on Hugging Face every few weeks. But BYOK doesn't cover code completions, embeddings, or repository indexing. So when does running a local model actually pay off? 

Alpha Romer Coma is benchmarking three open-weight coders on a single RTX 4090 and an Apple M5 chip against GitHub Copilot's default agent mode on real repository tasks, reporting time to first token, tool-call accuracy, and task completion rate. In this session, you'll see which workload patterns on real tasks favor a local GPU, which favor Copilot out of the box, and you'll learn how to run the same comparison on your own repositories.
