He has helped shape the future of agentic workflows on GitHub, collaborating closely with the open source community and industry pioneers. Outside of tech, Sam is a former professional drummer and enjoys blen

abstract:
Extending and customizing GitHub Copilot is now easier than ever!

In this session you'll learn how to discover exactly what agent skills, plugins, and MCP servers you need via a powerful, new AI agent resource search. You'll also see how to setup once and run your connections everywhere. These new features are easy to use and help you avoid manually managing JSON configuration.

Whether you use the GitHub Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, or Copilot in github.com, you can discover, authorize once, and instantly use your favorite services like Sentry, Cloudflare, Notion, Microsoft 365, Azure, Figma, and more, anywhere you use Copilot. And on shared workstations, signing out of Copilot automatically revokes access to your connected services.

Join us for a first look at a simpler way to connect Copilot to the tools you rely on.

title: Security by default: a maintainer’s wishlist for GitHub Actions v2
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: William Woodruff
speakers.title: Member of Technical Staff
speakers.bio:
William is a Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, working on high-performance and secure Python tooling. He previously worked at Astral on the same tooling, and prior to that was an Engineering Director at Trail of Bits, where he ran a team responsible for high-impact security contributions to open source ecosystems.

Outside of work, William is the primary maintainer of zizmor, one of the maintainers of Homebrew, and a long-term contributor to Python packaging (PyPA, PyPI) and Python cryptography.

abstract:
GitHub Actions has a reputation for insecure defaults. This session takes that reputation seriously and covers questions that follow from it. First, in 2026, how are teams closing the gap between the platform's defaults and the security posture they actually want? And second, how can GitHub ship the security features that make Actions the default choice for the next decade without losing the openness that makes it accessible to contributors and newcomers?

Along the way, you'll get a fast tour of Actions' best-known footguns and their fixes, a look at how attacker behavior has shifted over the past year, and an honest picture of what a security-by-default "v2" of GitHub Actions could look like.

title: The human side of AI: How building community drove 94% Copilot adoption

speakers.name: Brittany Istenes
speakers.title: OSS strategist/Community Architect
speakers.bio:
Brittany Istenes began her career as an elementary school educator before forging a path into technology. She has led OSS advisory councils, special interest groups, open source contributions, community building, InnerSource initiatives, and all the gray areas in between. Today, Brittany shares these practices across the financial services industry and global technology community. Her goal is to create frictionless developer-centric environments where collaboration, trust, and innovation thrive.

She has built and scaled open source advisory councils, ambassador programs, and enterprise contri

abstract: What if scaling AI isn’t about better models, but better human connection? Learn how a large U.S.-based financial services firm achieved 94% GitHub Copilot adoption and 78% agent-written code by combining grassroots engagement, storytelling, and innersource, making AI something developers wanted to use and build together. This session shares how treating AI adoption as a people challenge drives trust, plus how to measure meaningful adoption through impact.

title: What happens behind the scenes when you run npm install

speakers.name: Karen Li
speakers.title: Software Engineer III
speakers.bio: Karen is a software engineer on GitHub’s npm team with a unique path from concert pianist to elementary school teacher to technologist. She brings a teaching mindset to engineering, making complex systems easier to understand, and shares insights at the intersection of education and technology. Her motto, “I invest in brains,” reflects her commitment to learning and empowering others.

abstract:
Every npm install pulls in code from a sprawling network of packages, maintainers, and automation you've never met and mostly can't see. So what are you actually trusting when you run it?

This talk traces a single npm install down to what it really depends on: who can publish a package, what stops them from shipping something malicious, and where those safeguards break. You'll see how recent attacks slipped through, what npm audit does and doesn't catch, and how provenance and OpenID Connect (OIDC) now let you verify that a package was built by who it claims.

You'll leave with a mental model for reading the risk in your own dependency tree, and a few concrete checks to run before you trust the next package you pull in.

title: What open source can teach us about agents in CI/CD

speakers.name: Jorge Castro
speakers.title: Open Source Community Engineer and Developer Relations
speakers.bio: Jorge O. Castro is a community engineer specializing in open source, with a focus on engineering, contributor health, and end-user advocacy. He demonstrates the business value of open source to some of the world’s largest companies so they can support developers and help keep the modern world running sustainably.

abstract:
What happens when you build an operating system the way you build an application? Jorge Castro uses projectbluefin.io to show how container images, CI/CD, GitOps, and open source projects can work together in a reproducible software supply chain. 

The session starts with a pipeline that builds and publishes a containerized operating system. From there, Jorge shows where agents can help: generating or updating configuration, responding to changes in the pipeline, and working with the tools that build and deliver the system. He’ll also cover the limits of this approach, including how teams keep changes reviewable, traceable, and safe to reproduce. 

You’ll leave with a concrete pattern for adding agents to an existing CI/CD workflow without treating AI as a replacement for the pipeline, its controls, or the people reviewing its changes.

title: Goodbye, tutorial hell: AI guides and the new documentation layer

speakers.name: Erin Mikail Staples
speakers.title: Staff Developer Experience Engineer
speakers.bio:
Erin is a seasoned developer experience engineer who has spent her career arguing that “read the docs and hope” isn’t a learning strategy. At Tiger Data, she serves as a voice of the user, leading developer education and shaping the docs, tutorials, and tooling engineers reach for instead of dread.

A contributor and maintainer to open source projects across the data and AI ecosystem, Erin has also taught as an adjunct instructor at NYU’s Graduate School of Arts and Science. She geeks out on the intersection of AI, developer education, and the unglamorous work of filtering signal from noise.

speakers.name: Janice Niemeir
speakers.title: Director, Docs Engagement & Experience
speakers.bio: Janice hangs out at the intersection of technical content, systems & platforms for publishing words, and managing teams towards independence. Before GitHub she taught International Baccalaureate theatre in central Phoenix, worked for a company that put play spaces in public libraries, and got into tech through an Outreachy internship and open source work with Gulp. She moved her family and dog to Amsterdam five years ago and loves that she doesn't have to drive anymore.

abstract:
For years, "developer education" has meant read the docs and hope. And most MCP servers are just API wrappers with extra steps. What if the server could teach instead? 

When an AI agent in GitHub Copilot or another MCP-compatible editor reads documentation through an opinionated MCP server, it stops giving generic advice and starts teaching the way your product is meant to be used.  

Claire Waters and Erin Mikail Staples show the difference live: you'll fork an open source reference server, install it in your editor, and watch agent behavior change side by side. You'll leave with a working scaffold you can adapt for your own product or codebase.

title: Beyond the code: How Forge powers the rest of the SDLC

speakers.name: Kevin Kennedy
speakers.title: Principal Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Kevin is a Principal Software Architect at Micron, where he develops shared libraries and platforms that improve developer productivity. During his 12 years with the company, he has worked closely with teams building software for Micron’s manufacturing operations to identify and solve common development challenges.

speakers.name: Josh McIntosh
speakers.title: Senior Software Development Manager
speakers.bio: Josh McIntosh leads globally distributed teams that build the software that keeps manufacturing running. During his 21 years in the industry — including the last 15 spent leading engineering teams through complex business challenges — he has learned how to turn difficult technical challenges into shipped solutions across distributed, cross-cultural teams. Outside of work, Josh enjoys camping, hiking, and fishing with his family and dogs in the Idaho mountains.

abstract:
GitHub Copilot changed how developers at Micron write code, but the team saw a larger opportunity in applying AI across the entire software development lifecycle. Engineering teams went all-in on Copilot, leveraging its full capabilities and partnering closely with Microsoft to help shape new features based on real-world enterprise needs.  

This session introduces Forge, an AI-powered engineering platform that drives measurable gains in productivity, quality, and speed by extending Copilot beyond coding to enable agentic workflows across planning, development, testing, documentation, and delivery. You’ll see exactly how one shared platform can replace duplicate, team-by-team agent efforts, along with how to treat context as shared infrastructure for agentic work.

title: Admin readiness for AI usage management

speakers.name: Abel Berhane
speakers.title: Sr Service Delivery Engineer
speakers.bio:
Abel Berhane is a technology leader and engineer who helps organizations turn emerging AI capabilities into practical, scalable ways of working. In his work with GitHub Expert Services, he has led and contributed to enterprise initiatives involving GitHub Copilot adoption, developer enablement, agentic software development, and technical transformation. His work helps customers embed new tools effectively throughout the software development lifecycle. 

Abel’s background spans DevOps, cloud engineering, automation, and developer productivity. He has designed and delivered strategic planning en

speakers.name: Vanessa Minik
speakers.title: Senior Service Delivery Engineer
speakers.bio:
Vanessa helps organizations turn AI from an exciting technology into something people can actually use in their day-to-day development workflows. As a Senior Service Delivery Engineer on GitHub's Expert Learning Services team, she focuses on GitHub Copilot adoption and enablement, helping teams rethink how they build software in an increasingly AI-native world.

With several years at GitHub across customer enablement, technical training, and solution development, Vanessa has a practical perspective on both the technology and the people side of AI adoption. She's especially interested in agenti

abstract:
Enterprise administrators are increasingly expected to explain Copilot adoption, spending, and governance to leadership, finance, and security. In this interactive workshop, participants step into the role of a Copilot administrator responding to three realistic stakeholder inquiries.

Using enterprise and organization scenarios, attendees will explore how to assess usage and adoption, understand how spending maps to the organization, and review the policies and access decisions that shape Copilot management. They will practice navigating administrative settings, interpreting organizational data, understanding the scope of controls, and preparing clear responses for each stakeholder group.

The session concludes with a practical action plan focused on adoption, spending, and governance. Participants leave with a repeatable playbook for answering executive questions and making informed Copilot administration decisions across the enterprise.

title: Beyond pass or fail: How agents verify AI-generated code (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Jeff An
speakers.title: CTO & Co-founder
speakers.bio:
Jeff An is the co-founder and CTO of Momentic, a San Francisco-based startup that automates software testing with AI. Momentic executes millions of tests per month and is trusted by top-tier engineering teams including Notion, Bilt, Retool, Xero, and 100 more.

Before starting Momentic, Jeff was the youngest tech lead at Robinhood, where he led the developer experience team as the company grew 300%.

abstract:
Your coding agent just shipped a feature. The tests pass, but does the feature work as intended? 

This session shows how agents can go beyond scripted checks to explore an application in a real browser, investigate unexpected behavior, and keep tests current as the product changes. You’ll see how they gather evidence, reproduce failures, and distinguish product bugs from broken tests or infrastructure problems. 

You’ll also learn how deterministic controls keep agents within safe boundaries, and leave with a practical framework for deciding what agents should test, what code should control, and when a human needs to step in.

title: Building domain-specific AI agents for hardware reliability at NVIDIA

speakers.name: Maria Victoria Gromysch
speakers.title: Test Engineer
speakers.bio:
Maria Gromysh is a Test Systems Engineer focused on bridging AI, software, and large-scale hardware validation. With a background in electrical and computer engineering and experience at NVIDIA and AMD, she has led cross-functional efforts in firmware validation, production test readiness, and system-level debugging. 

Her recent work focuses on how AI agents and LLM-based systems can improve engineering productivity, including code review automation, failure diagnosis, and manufacturing test optimization. Maria is passionate about scaling intelligent infrastructure and turning complex hardwar

abstract:
GitHub Copilot catches surface-level issues. But what about hardware-specific constraints, firmware interactions, and system-level failures? For teams working on hardware-software systems, AI adoption is significantly more complex than in pure software environments.

Maria Victoria Gromysch shares a practical framework developed at NVIDIA for integrating AI across the full engineering lifecycle: test generation at pre-commit, AI-assisted code review at commit time, and system validation in CI/CD.

You'll also learn how to build domain-specific agents trained on internal logs and diagnostics, design a layered AI workflow, identify where general-purpose tools fall short, and close the feedback loop between production failures and model improvement.

title: Opening the black box: Tracing, debugging, and fixing your GitHub Actions agents (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Serge Dybskiy
speakers.title: Developer Experience Engineer
speakers.bio: Sergiy is a software developer with 12+ years of experience. He's on a journey to learn how to communicate effectively about developer tooling. Through workshops, videos, and blog posts—and by building with AI himself—he's exploring how to make complex tools easier to understand and adopt.

abstract: GitHub Actions has become home to a whole generation of custom agents: triaging issues, iterating on pull requests, reviewing diffs. But when one misbehaves, you get a green check or a red X and nothing else. Agent tracing from Sentry show you what actually happened: which tool calls errored, how long each step of the workflow took, how many tokens got consumed, and where to optimize next. Connect Copilot to Sentry's MCP server to pull that data on demand, or build your own automations with Sentry as the source of production agent traces for evals and debugging. You'll leave this session knowing how to turn a silent pass/fail into a full trace you can debug, and how to feed real production data back into improving your agents.

title: Scaling GitHub’s infrastructure for how developers build today

speakers.name: Brian Celenza
speakers.title: Principal Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Brian Celenza is a Principal Software Engineer at GitHub, where he works on the storage and services that power every git push and git clone. He has spent two decades building software and cloud infrastructure across developer productivity, healthcare, and commerce. Brian is now helping rebuild GitHub’s Git infrastructure to support workloads at agent scale. Outside of work, he enjoys hiking, gardening, cooking, and baking.

abstract: We share how GitHub is evolving its infrastructure to take on more concurrent work from developers, automations, and agents. That evolution includes a new storage architecture for Git repository data. Explore the engineering behind this work, the journey it's taken to get there, what it means for your teams, and how it strengthens GitHub's foundation for the next generation of software development.

title: Stop prompting, start delegating: Configure Copilot to own the work

speakers.name: Ken Muse
speakers.title: Staff DevOps Architect | ODST | FDE
speakers.bio: Ken is a Staff DevOps Architect on the ODST team at GitHub. He is a four-time Microsoft Azure MVP (retired) and a Microsoft Certified Trainer, and he was both an ALM | DevOps Ranger and a member of the Microsoft Azure Advisors. Ken is a frequent community speaker and has appeared at GitHub Universe, VSLive!, Live! 360, DevOps World, SQLSaturday, All Day DevOps, Global Azure, and TAG DevOps panels. When not speaking or coding, Ken enjoys playing multiple instruments and composing.

speakers.name: Mickey Gousset
speakers.title: Staff DevOps Architect | ODST | FDE
speakers.bio: Mickey is a staff DevOps architect at GitHub. He is passionate about DevOps and helping developers achieve their goals. Mickey speaks on topics at various user groups, code camps, and conferences around the world.

abstract:
Your repository's Copilot configuration may be all that stands between you and trusting AI to handle complex tasks on its own. In this session, Ken Muse and Mickey Gousset demonstrate how to enhance a TypeScript app by layering GitHub Copilot's full stack, showing how each capability reinforces the last. 

You'll see exactly how Copilot spends context and tokens, with before-and-after comparisons that make the efficiency gains measurable. You'll leave with a working project and an understanding of which Copilot capability fits which task, so you can delegate more and prompt less.

title: The view from the labs: What's next for AI-assisted development

speakers.name: April Leonard
speakers.title: VP of Engineering for GitHub Copilot
speakers.bio: April Leonard is VP of Engineering for GitHub Copilot, leading the teams responsible for the platform, infrastructure, and product experiences behind AI-powered software development. She focuses on bringing advanced AI capabilities to developers while meeting the reliability, security, and governance requirements of the world's largest enterprises.

speakers.name: Richard Seroter
speakers.title: Senior Director and Chief Evangelist
speakers.bio: Richard Seroter is a Senior Director and Chief Evangelist at Google Cloud, where he leads teams shaping the future of software development. He oversees products and engineering for Google’s flagship languages and frameworks, including Go, Dart, Flutter, and Genkit. He also leads the company’s Open Source Program Office, Developer Relations, and Documentation programs. A longtime architect and author, Richard shares daily AI and cloud expertise at seroter.com and on X at @rseroter.

speakers.name: Angela Jiang
speakers.title: Head of Product, Claude Platform
speakers.bio: Angela Jiang is the Head of Product for the Claude Platform at Anthropic, including model APIs, hyperscaler integrations, agentic infrastructure, and connectivity controls for businesses as well as Anthropic’s own product infrastructure. Before joining Anthropic, she was Head of Product for the API Platform at OpenAI and led embedded payments at Stripe.

abstract: The people building frontier AI models see early signals about where capabilities are heading and which skills and workflows are about to matter more or require a shift. This interactive panel brings together leaders from the major frontier model labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google Cloud) that power GitHub Copilot for the conversation developers actually want: a candid, forward-looking discussion about what the next two years of AI-assisted development look like, and what that means for the people in the room.

title: Visa's Zero-Secrets Initiative: no hardcoded secrets, no exceptions
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Kautilay Siingh
speakers.title: Security Architect
speakers.bio: Kautilay is a Security Architect focused on payment security, working closely with engineering teams to build secure-by-design systems at scale. With a background in application security, he brings a pragmatic approach to integrating security into fast-paced development environments. At Visa, he collaborates across teams to secure critical payment products used globally. Outside of work, he enjoys casual gaming, security deep dives, and CTF walkthroughs.

speakers.name: Sanjeev Murthy
speakers.title: Director, Cybersecurity
speakers.bio:
Sanjeev Murthy is Director of Security Architecture at Visa, where he leads security architecture reviews and assessments for one of the world’s most complex, highly regulated, always-on payment networks. He oversees security assessments across critical platforms, helping teams design and deliver solutions that meet Visa’s transaction-grade security and compliance standards. 

Sanjeev works closely with engineering and product teams to embed security early, automate risk management, and help teams ship secure solutions at global scale.

abstract:
Visa’s policy is simple: no credentials in source code, ever. Turning that into something that actually runs across a global engineering organization took a full procedure, not a feature toggle.

This session walks the path end to end. First, detection: automated scanning for credentials across our whole estate. Next, the procedure we built around it: how alerts get routed and prioritized, who owns a finding, and why the fix is revoking and rotating the credential rather than only deleting the line of code. Then, prevention: stopping a push that carries a secret, and the governed exception path that sits alongside it. And throughout, how automation cuts the alert load, with AI assisting on the human side of a finding rather than on the secret itself.

Enforcing a zero secrets policy at scale is a massive operational challenge. You will leave this session with the sequence we used, what we learned along the way, and the parts that can be reused in your own organization.

title: GitHub configuration as code: Scaling org management with Terraform

speakers.name: Yasuhiro Osaki
speakers.title: Software Engineer
speakers.bio:
Yasuhiro is a Software Engineer at Sony, where he has spent over a decade driving GitHub adoption and serving as GitHub Owner across the organization. Sony’s development landscape spans embedded software to web and cloud applications, and he has developed enterprise-specific strategies for GitHub utilization at scale. 

In the past year alone, Yasuhiro helped grow GitHub Enterprise Cloud users from 4,000 to 7,000 and GitHub Copilot users from 900 to 4,000. He currently advises multiple organizations as a GitHub Enterprise Owner. He holds three GitHub Certifications (Actions, Admin, and GitHub

abstract:
As organizations scale, GitHub configurations can become increasingly complex to manage. Restrict admin access too tightly and development slows. Loosen it too much and security risks increase.

This session shows how one team solved this by codifying critical GitHub configurations through Terraform, with every change proposed and reviewed through pull requests. Over three years, more than 800 configuration changes have been managed through this model, preserving both governance and developer autonomy.

You'll learn how to manage configurations, automate routine requests with Copilot, ensure traceability and governance for every change through pull request-based workflows, and leverage accumulated IaC knowledge for practical AI agent adoption.

title: AI agents write the code. Novus decides what to build next.  (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Tiffany Kitchen
speakers.title: Head of Product
speakers.bio: Tiffany Kitchen is Head of Product for Novus at Pendo. Over the past decade, she has built a career spanning engineering and product. Beginning as an engineer at the CIA, Tiffany helped establish the agency’s first product management role before stepping into it herself. She later served as Director of Product at Anno.ai and then spent several years building Pendo Analytics before moving into her current role leading product development for Novus.

abstract: Coding agents can write and ship software quickly, but teams still need to know what to build and which user problems matter most. In this demo, Pendo’s Head of Product shows how Novus, the product agent that connects user behavior to the codebase, identifies product opportunities, finds UX issues, and recommends what teams and coding agents should work on next. You’ll see Novus turn product signals into action: surfacing an issue, proposing a fix, and connecting that work to the codebase. This demo also shows how to use AI to move from product discovery to development, while keeping teams focused on the updates that users care about.

title: The 2am RCA Agent: Architecting AI that investigates, not hallucinates

speakers.name: Achin Gupta
speakers.title: Staff Software Engineer
speakers.bio:
Achin Gupta makes AI agents observable and debuggable. A Staff Engineer at Intuit, he builds distributed observability backends on Kubernetes instrumented with OpenTelemetry, helping teams understand complex systems. 

Over the past nine years, he has tackled all kinds of challenges: from slow services to AI agents that confidently do the wrong thing. He developed a spec-driven methodology for AI-assisted coding that keeps humans accountable and has used it to win AI hackathons by delivering production-quality systems in under eight hours. 

An upcoming CNCF speaker and presenter at All Things

speakers.name: Divya Mahajan
speakers.title: Software Development Engineer
speakers.bio:
Divya Mahajan is a Software Development Engineer at Amazon Alexa, where she builds production-grade agentic AI and LLM systems at scale. Her work sits at the intersection of conversational AI, agentic automation, and reliable system design, with a focus on accuracy, observability, and production readiness. 

She has led the development of LLM evaluation pipelines, prompt optimization strategies, and multi-turn agent workflows that serve Alexa+ users. Beyond her core role, Divya actively explores agentic automation and designs workflows, including multi-agent systems. 

Divya has won multiple A

abstract:
At 2 am, an alert fires. You spend 90 minutes jumping between Grafana, Jaeger, and logs, correlating by hand, fighting confirmation bias, and writing the RCA doc backwards. Achin Gupta and Divya Mahajan built an agent that does this in seconds. 

Surprisingly, the LLM only handles 4 of 10 nodes. Signal fetching, BFS topology traversal, correlation, and scoring are fully deterministic, which means they’re auditable, replayable, and cheap. The LLM narrates the evidence rather than gathering it. 

In this session, you'll see the architecture, a live demo of an alert-to-RCA report in seconds, and the design principles that make the system trustworthy in production. All code is open source; the paper is published on Zenodo. You'll leave with a blueprint for building agents you can actually trust in the middle of the night.

title: When a prototype becomes critical, does your GitHub policy know? (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Baruch Sadogursky
speakers.title: Head of Developer Relations
speakers.bio:
Baruch Sadogursky (@jbaruch) worked with Java before it had generics, practiced DevOps before Docker existed, and built developer relations before it had a name. He built JFrog’s DevRel function as the company grew from 10 people through its initial public offering. Baruch co-authored "Liquid Software" and "DevOps Tools for Java Developers" and is a Java Champion, Microsoft MVP, and CNCF Ambassador alum. 

Today, Baruch is obsessed with how AI agents write code. At Tessl, an AI agent enablement platform, he works on engineering, managing, and sharing context with agents. He also shares his kno

abstract:
What happens when a prototype goes into production and starts handling real customer payments, but its GitHub repository still carries the merge requirements it launched with? 

In this session, Baruch Sadogursky shares how he syncs ownership and business criticality from Port into GitHub as custom properties, making it possible to find repositories by owning team and point a GitHub ruleset at critical services. 

You'll watch that gap close live, and leave with a repeatable pattern: Port supplies the context, and GitHub turns that context into enforced policy.

title: Resolve your security alerts faster with GitHub Copilot
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Carlin Cherry
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: Carlin is a Senior Product Manager at GitHub, working on Dependabot and the software supply chain. With a unique background that combines data science and software engineering experience, she brings technical depth and user empathy to vulnerability management. In her role, Carlin leads efforts to make security integrate seamlessly into developer workflows, helping organizations prioritize what matters most. Outside of work, she is a board member of her alma mater, Rice University (go Owls!), and a member of the ThinkCyber Foundation. She also enjoys running and plays board games competitively.

speakers.name: Jon Janego
speakers.title: Senior Product Manager
speakers.bio: Jon is a senior product manager on the GitHub code security team and has been working in the information security industry as a product manager and practitioner for over 15 years. He lives in Chicago.

abstract:
Security debt keeps growing: more code, more tools, more pressure to ship fast. Most teams are staring at an alert backlog nobody has time to work through.

Agentic autofix helps you reduce the amount of time it takes to resolve your security alerts. It generates mergeable fixes for them in minutes, so remediation becomes a pull request review instead of a multi-day investigation.

In this session, you'll see it in action through a live demo, plus what we've learned from our customers using it. You'll leave knowing how to put it to work in your own workflow.

title: What's worth building when AI can build anything?

speakers.name: Kent C. Dodds
speakers.title: Product Engineer
speakers.bio: Kent C. Dodds is a world renowned web development educator and engineer. He's actively involved in the open source community. He is the creator of EpicProduct.engineer, EpicWeb.dev, EpicAI.pro, EpicReact.dev, and TestingJavaScript.com. He also built Kody, an open-source personal software ecosystem for multi-agent work. He's a Microsoft MVP, GitHub Star, instructor on egghead.io and Frontend Masters, live streamer, and podcaster. Kent is married and the father of six kids and he lives in Utah.

speakers.name: Sue Black
speakers.title: Professor of Computer Science and Technology Evangelist
speakers.bio:
Professor Sue Black OBE is an award-winning computer scientist, technology leader and social entrepreneur, passionate about using technology to create positive change. A Professor of Computer Science at Durham University, she is best known for leading the successful campaign to save Bletchley Park and for founding initiatives including BCSWomen, #techmums and TechUPWomen, supporting women and underserved communities into technology careers.
Named one of Forbes’ Top 50 Women in Tech globally, Sue was awarded an OBE for services to technology and named Everywoman’s Tech for Good Award winner in

abstract:
AI can build almost anything you ask it to, which makes a harder question unavoidable: what's actually worth building? In this conversation, Sue Black of Durham University and Kent C. Dodds of kody.codes make the case for building deliberately rather than reflexively. 

This session will explore what responsible software looks like and take a deeper dive into the daily reality of shipping, choosing between tools, and maintaining what’s already built. You'll leave with a sharper set of questions to bring to your own work, along with a clearer sense of when speed is worth it and when it isn't.

title: IBM Neo: From specifications to verified software delivery (Sponsored)

speakers.name: Miha Kralj
speakers.title: Global CTO, IBM Consulting Microsoft Practice

speakers.name: Josh Scriven
speakers.title: Microsoft Americas Practice, AI Leader
speakers.bio: Microsoft Americas Practice AI Leader at IBM Consulting, where he focuses on scaling AI‑assisted and agent‑driven development across large enterprise organizations. He works closely with GitHub and Microsoft teams to integrate Copilot, automation, and governance‑first patterns into real‑world software engineering and modernization efforts. Josh helps enterprises move beyond experimentation to repeatable, production‑ready AI development models that balance developer velocity with operational control.

abstract: See how IBM Neo brings together specification-driven development, AI agents, and proof-based validation across the software delivery lifecycle. In this live demo, learn how teams set direction, evaluate evidence, and intervene at key decision points while agents work toward verifiable outcomes.

title: Delete the wiki: An MCP platform that closes its own loop

speakers.name: Sumanth Mothkuri
speakers.title: Sr. Platform Engineer
speakers.bio:
Sumanth Mothkuri is a problem solver who turns toil into automation. An SRE turned Platform Engineer and now evolving into an AI Engineer, he has spent five years building the unglamorous plumbing that keeps engineers shipping in one of the most regulated environments in tech, including pipelines, monitoring systems, and agentic workflows. 

As a Senior Platform Engineer at Equifax, Sumanth works across GCP, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Terraform, and the agent stack, including ADK, MCP integrations, and custom AI agents. His background as a full-stack developer informs how he builds for the human

speakers.name: Hrushikesh Pokala
speakers.title: Sr Software Engineer - Lead
speakers.bio:
Living at the heart of the AI revolution, Hrushikesh Pokala brings 12 years of experience in software development and recently completed a master’s degree in Data Analytics. Their expertise spans deep learning and neural networks, fueled by a passion for building intelligent systems that actually work. 

When not training models, Hrushikesh enjoy perfecting their backhand on the table tennis court and exploring America’s backroads. Having driven a Tesla through nearly every state, they are as comfortable navigating cross-country charging networks as they are navigating complex datasets.

abstract:
Wikis promise discoverability. Portals promise self-service. Both start rotting the moment a story closes and the docs stop matching reality.

So the team stopped writing docs by hand and built a platform that writes them itself: an MCP-powered loop where AI agents read live infrastructure context to ship real work, then write that context back the moment a story is done, as docs, diagrams, tech-debt records, and follow-up tasks. The documentation stays current because producing it is part of doing the work, not a chore that happens after.

This session will demo the full loop end to end: provisioning a codespace from intent, then watching the agent ship the change, file the docs, log the tech debt, and refresh the architecture diagram on its own. You'll leave with the patterns that make a platform self-healing instead of self-rotting, and a clear sense of how to close the loop between doing the work and documenting it on your own stack.

title: From AI-assisted work to agent-enabled delivery: Scaling AI across product teams

speakers.name: Brendan Bergen

Today, he leads Vanguard’s efforts to integrate AI across the software development lifecycle, helping teams work smarter, move faster, and ship with confidence. Brendan has presented at multiple conferences, including Oracle OpenWorld 2018, Vanguard Unlimited 2023, and Vanguard Unlimited 2024.

He is passionate about turning emerging AI capabilities into practical, governed platforms that help thousands of engineers deliver faster and with confidence.

abstract:
What if scaling AI across product teams worked like a game: moving through levels, unlocking criteria, and progressing clearly? Vanguard is improving how more than 800 cross-functional product teams operate by applying a structured AI maturity framework across the product development lifecycle.

This session shares where the team is now, the capabilities being scaled today, and lessons on how organizations can progress from AI-assisted work toward agent-enabled delivery.

speakers.name: Madelyn Tarr
speakers.bio:

She is currently focused on automating safe rollouts through APIs, MCP, and other emerging tools. 

Before joining Amplitude, Madelyn worked at a startup, which taught her what it takes to ship quickly. She enjoys building systems that reduce friction for teams and digging into user behavior to understand the people and stories behind how products are used.

abstract: Coding agents can help teams ship features in hours, but a fast release doesn’t tell you whether a change worked. This session introduces Statsig, a platform for managing feature gates, experiments, and product metrics, and shows how teams can use it to measure the impact of their releases. A live demo will illustrate how staged rollouts, guardrail metrics, experiments, and automated responses to regressions help teams learn from releases sooner—and what to do when a metric changes unexpectedly. You’ll leave with a practical approach for measuring release impact, catching regressions earlier, and making better decisions about what to ship next.

Originally from Melbourne, he now lives in San Francisco and spends his weekends exploring

Before that, he co-founded Chef in 2008 and spent a decade as its CTO, helping bring configuration management, infrastructure as code, and DevOps into the world. He calls himself a practical technologist, writes regularly at adamhjk.com about being an “absolute AI maximalist,” and is one of the loudest public voices arguing that the future of software engineering is building the machine that builds the machine.

abstract:
Peer review was how engineers learned: juniors got sharper, seniors stayed honest. Then agents wrote the code, and reviewing each other turned into auditing machines. That's why it felt awful. 

On separate teams, Adam Jacob and Dylan Ratcliffe each found the same fix: stop reviewing the code and review the plan a human writes before the agent builds. The human loop came back, and now they enjoy the work again.  

This talk is the two of them comparing notes and disagreeing hard on one thing: whether review stops mattering once software is no longer a garden you tend for people. You'll leave knowing how to move review upstream on your own team, with a clear view of what you keep and what you give up.

After review and deployment, the team checks error rates and SLOs for regressions. You’ll leave with a practical model for verifying agent-written changes and deciding where human review, escalation, and a kill switch belong.

title: Open PRs, don't merge them: Fine-grained authorization for hosted MCP servers
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Nick Taylor
speakers.title: Developer Advocate/Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Nick is a Microsoft MVP, GitHub Star, AAIF Ambassador, AWS Community Builder, and Developer Advocate at Pomerium. He has over two decades of experience in technology and a decade in open source, with six years of professional open source work at OpenSauced, dev.to, Netlify, and now Pomerium. You’ll often find him live streaming tech content, either solo or with friends from the community.

abstract:
Hosted MCP servers all work the same way: OAuth in, broad scope out. One global toggle decides which tools to expose, and every authenticated identity gets the full set. So every agent inherits everything its human can do.

Teams often want something more precise. Maybe an agent should open a pull request and leave the merge to a human. Today the upstream server can't express that, and you can't change it, because it isn't yours.

This session shows a pattern that works today: an identity-aware proxy that adds per-identity authorization in front of any hosted MCP server, no changes upstream. You'll see it live — Copilot opening a PR and leaving the merge to a reviewer, enforced per user — and you'll leave with a working pattern for the MCP servers your team already depends on.

topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

abstract: For the past six years, the GitHub Security Lab has worked to secure the open source ecosystem, and that work has surfaced a set of practical principles that hold up in the real world. The speakers will share what succeeded, what didn't, and the ideas that matter most. Keep it simple, so security is easy for developers to understand and implement. Make it delicious, so security improvements are something people actually want to adopt. And keep it social, because nothing beats the collective intelligence of the community, especially now that agents and skills can tap into and magnify that shared knowledge. The session closes by looking at how the recent wave of AI is reshaping open source security, and what the future looks like in that new world. You'll leave with principles you can apply to make security stick in your own projects and communities.

title: AI, Actions, and tooling: Coinbase's move to GitHub with data residency

abstract:

GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency met that bar. This session shares how Coinbase made the move.

You'll see how the team migrated 10,000+ repositories with near-zero disruption, maintaining strict compliance throughout by building a custom GitHub Actions pipeline and deploying an AI agent that drove 99% self-service across the migration. The result: developers kept shipping, and the organization stayed compliant, start to finish.

You'll leave knowing how to scale to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency in a regulated environment: the tooling, the automation, and the practices that keep developers productive and compliance intact along the way.

An engineer by training, Anirudh has worked across enterprise technology, strategy, and go-to-market, including roles at Cisco spanning cloud, security, AI infrastructure, and emerging technology. Outside of work, he enjoys swimming and exploring Bay

abstract: AI agents now push code at machine speed, and a single rogue agent or stolen identity can wipe a repo, overwrite history, or delete releases in seconds. And GitHub is no longer just code. It's your Issues, Actions, Projects, and Wikis, part of a broader DevOps workflow that spans Azure DevOps, Jira, and Confluence. Native controls like rulesets and immutable releases are your first line of defense, but version history isn't a backup either; it can be wiped alongside the code and pipelines it's meant to protect. This session digs into a threat most teams haven't considered and are dangerously unprepared for. Then, in a live demo, we'll recover code after an attack from the clean, isolated backups Rubrik automates. You'll leave understanding why traditional version history won't save you, and what real resilience for your entire DevOps workflow actually looks like.

This interactive session gives you a practical way to handle the flood. You'll learn how to make your SECURITY.md actually reduce noise, use the latest private vulnerability reporting features to route reports where they belong, and get interactive with prototype triage tools that GitHub Security Lab is building right now.

title: Your CI has full internet access. GitHub Actions firewall changes that.
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Zach Steindler
speakers.title: Principal Engineer
speakers.bio: Zach is the chair of the OpenSSF Technical Advisory Council and co-chair of the Securing Repositories Working Group, which helps coordinate security improvements in programming language package repositories like PyPI and RubyGems. He works at GitHub on securing software development for open source and enterprises. Away from computers, he enjoys gardening and welding.

abstract:
Your GitHub Actions workflows have full access to the public internet. This is great for pulling dependencies. But it's a problem when you need to know exactly what your build reached out to. After an incident, can you say which URLs a workflow hit? Can you stop it from talking to anything you didn't approve?

GitHub Actions firewall sits between your workflows and the public internet. It records every outbound request, tracks which process made it, and lets you allow only the traffic you actually want, so a compromised dependency can't quietly phone home, and you have an audit trail when you need one.

In this session, you'll see how to turn it on, read the traffic it captures, and write allowlists that fit your builds.

topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

abstract:
Platform teams are being asked to do more with AI and fewer hands, but the maintenance never stops: version bumps, bug fixes, security findings, and a steady stream of vendor releases all keep coming.

Enter the second shift. This session walks through a pattern where a night shift of GitHub Copilot cloud agents maintains the same self-hosted GitHub Actions infrastructure they run on. You'll see a night in the life of that crew: agents that clock in, proactively update dependencies, read release notes and vendor blogs, open PRs, classify operational changes by risk, and auto-deploy the changes that policy already approves, escalating the rest to a human.

You'll leave with a concrete pattern for putting Copilot agents to work on your own platform maintenance: what they can safely own overnight, how to gate risky changes behind policy, and how to keep humans in control of everything that matters.

abstract: When you use GitHub Copilot in auto mode, it routes each task to the model best suited for it, and that routing changes as the task changes. But how does it decide? You'll see a live demo of auto selection in action, learn what signals drive routing decisions under the hood, and pick up best practices for context management and planning that help auto mode work even better for you.

abstract:

Seventeen specialized AI agents now handle requirements, spec generation, automated testing, security scanning, accessibility validation, and deployment, all connected to Jira, Confluence, and New Relic through MCP.

Every pull request is reviewed by 5 to 11 independent agents that automatically fix issues and commit back to the branch, and every workflow has human approval gates built in. The result is a development lifecycle where agents do the heavy, repetitive work and people stay in control of the decisions that matter.

This session shares the real story: the architecture behind the system, the lessons learned building it (including what didn't work at first), and a practical view of what a multi-agent SDLC means for enterprise teams. You'll leave understanding how the pieces fit together, where human oversight belongs, and how to think about adopting agents across your own lifecycle rather than in a single step.

abstract:
Application security often gets underprioritized in large enterprises, letting legacy vulnerabilities pile up under delivery pressure and a rising tide of AI-driven threats. In this session, Manulife shares how it strengthened its AppSec culture through clear communication, real-time security reporting, and GitHub-native controls.

By embedding immediate security feedback directly into GitHub, Manulife's teams remediated risk at speed and safely resolved over 90% of their vulnerabilities. You'll also see how GitHub features enable an auditable DevSecOps CI/CD pipeline that catches security and operational risks before they reach production.

You'll leave with a practical playbook for driving AppSec adoption across a large organization: the communication tactics, the real-time reporting that made risk visible, and the GitHub controls that turned a vulnerability backlog into a 90%-remediated one.

title: Lessons from building tech in a low-connectivity community

abstract:
Most software assumes fast internet, cloud sync, and always-on connectivity. For millions of users across Africa, that's not reality. In this session, Alex Junior Antwi shares what he learned building CarbonSight, an offline-first food carbon footprint tracker for low-connectivity communities in Ghana, including the architectural decisions, trade-offs, and surprises along the way.  

You'll see a fully offline live demo, get a look into the data sync and conflict resolution logic under the hood, and understand the UX decisions that low-connectivity forces you to make. Whether you're building for emerging markets or just want to write more resilient software, you'll leave with practical patterns for shipping tools that work when the cloud doesn't.

title: Make your Postgres agent-ready: Branching, isolation, and safer shipping

speakers.name: Andre Landgraf
speakers.title: Staff Developer Advocate
speakers.bio:
Andre is a developer from Germany with a passion for building for the web. Based in the Bay Area, he is a Staff Developer Advocate at Databricks and previously worked as a Senior Software Engineer at LinkedIn. He holds master's degrees in Information Systems and Computer Science. 

Outside of work, Andre brings the community together through All Things Web events in San Francisco.

abstract:
Giving agents access to real database infrastructure is risky: one wrong migration and production breaks. Database branching changes that.

When your Postgres database supports instant, isolated branches, agents can safely experiment on real schemas and data without touching production. This means safer experimentation, faster shipping, and preview environments that spin up automatically.

In this session, Andre Landgraf shows how branching and isolation work under the hood, how to set up agent-ready database environments using tools like MCP and GitHub Actions, plus a live demo of an agent managing a database branch end to end. You'll leave with a clear framework for making your own database infrastructure safe for agentic workflows.

title: MCP, skills, or custom agents: Picking the right tool for the job

speakers.name: Sam Basu
speakers.title: Lead Developer Advocate
speakers.bio:
Sam Basu is a technologist, author, speaker, Microsoft MVP, and Lead Developer Advocate at Uno Platform. With a strong background in software development, he now focuses on advocating modern development platforms and AI tools for cross-platform applications. 

Outside of work, Sam enjoys travel, fast cars, cricket, and culinary adventures. You can find him on the internet.

abstract: GitHub Copilot gives you MCP tools, skills, and custom agents. But when do you reach for which capability? In this Sandbox session, Sam Basu runs live demos that make the differences concrete. You'll leave with a decision framework for matching the right capability to the right task, whether you're working in an IDE or a terminal.

title: Discover, install, and manage agent skills from your terminal with gh skill
topics: Security (RASP, supply chain, threat modeling, vulnerability detection)

speakers.name: Tommaso Moro
speakers.title: Software Engineer III
speakers.bio: Tommaso Moro is a product-minded software engineer who loves building software that is well crafted and impactful. Based in London, he works on agents and MCP at GitHub, where he recently led the launch of gh skill. After studying Philosophy and Computer Science, Tommaso entered the startup world as a founding product engineer before joining GitHub. That background gives him a unique perspective on software that extends beyond just the code. Outside the terminal, he enjoys tinkering with side projects, running, playing ultimate frisbee, and making music.

abstract:
Agent skills make agentic workflows far more capable, but discovering, installing, and managing them across environments can be a manual, fragmented process. gh skill fixes that.

In this live demo, you’ll see the new gh skill command end to end: finding skills, installing them into your agent, and managing them, all from your terminal. Then, you’ll go under the hood on how it’s built and learn how we’re using Git primitives and agent skill frontmatter to build a smarter and more secure ecosystem.

You'll leave knowing how to add gh skill to your own workflow and what to look for in a skill before you trust it with your agent.

title: A pixel dog that writes songs: Lessons from my first MCP server

speakers.name: Yunika Liu
speakers.title: Product Builder
speakers.bio: Yunika Liu is an independent product builder with a background in AEC SaaS customer enablement, where she helped thousands of users worldwide adopt complex software and introduced nontechnical audiences to practical MCP use cases. Today, she creates playful, human-centered AI experiences, including a pixel-art dog that lives on her desk, keeps her focused, and composes songs. She believes the best developer tools do more than process commands; they make technology feel personal, useful, and alive.

abstract:
It’s 2 a.m. You’re deep in a solo coding session. The terminal doesn’t care if you’re tired. Your IDE doesn’t notice you haven’t moved in an hour. But the golden retriever on your desk does. It tilts its head, nudges you with a Pomodoro timer, and when you finally ship that feature, it wags its tail and writes you a song.

Yunika Liu isn’t a backend engineer; she builds products that make complex systems feel personal. But using GitHub Copilot and its MCP support, she shipped the first version of Coco in a week. Coco is a pixel-art golden retriever that now lives in a floating desktop window and on a 64×64 LED display, powered by an MCP server with nine tools, 10 pixel animations, WebSocket sync, and music composition. In this talk, Yunika brings Coco onstage and shows how anyone can build their own MCP server. The only prerequisite is an idea weird enough to be worth building.

title: Beyond the repository: Using a migration to rethink how you build

speakers.name: Jon Clements

Jon Clements has led Chevron’s CI/CD DevOps team for eight years. He oversees the organization’s use of Azure DevOps and led its migration to GitHub. With more than 20 years of software experience, including roles at ExxonMobil and Boeing, Jon has spent the past 13 years at Chevron. He also contributed to Chevron’s migration of on-premises applications to the cloud and is now a primary contact for cloud adoption and modern software development practices. 

Jon also supports Chevron’s security strategy by selecting static and dynamic application security testing tools and helping design the com

speakers.name: Zachary Pollock
speakers.title: Sr. Software Engineer
speakers.bio: Zachary Pollock is a Senior Software Engineer at Chevron specializing in developer platforms, DevOps, and software delivery modernization. His work focuses on GitHub Enterprise, CI/CD pipelines, developer experience, and AI-powered development tools. Zach partners with engineering teams across Chevron to streamline software delivery, improve developer productivity, and implement enterprise-wide solutions.

abstract: Moving an engineering organization onto a new development platform is rarely just a tooling exercise. In this session, Jon Clements, DevOps and Enterprise Pipeline Manager, and Zachary Pollock, Senior Software Engineer—both at Chevron—share what the move to GitHub involved and why the work that mattered most sat outside the migration itself. You'll hear how an early-adopter community shaped the approach before the formal migration began and why sequencing let teams adopt new capabilities in stages. They also share what happened when emerging AI capabilities pushed the scope beyond development and into release, and how the team approached pipelines in GitHub Actions. Expect practical observations on change management, leadership alignment, and the importance of visibility, plus takeaways you can apply to your own migration, whether it’s finished, underway, or still being planned.

title: One CLI to replace your entire JavaScript toolchain

speakers.name: Alexander Lichter
speakers.title: Systems Engineer
speakers.bio: Alex is a Developer Relations Engineer at VoidZero (Cloudflare), a Nuxt.js team member, and open-source enthusiast. He creates tech-focused video content, speaks at conferences, and leads workshops that help developers grow their skills and advance the web ecosystem.

abstract:
The JavaScript ecosystem has long suffered from choice fatigue: picking a framework, deciding on a bundler, test runner, linter, and formatter, with each requiring its own setup and maintenance. 

What if one tool covered it all? Meet Vite+, the open source CLI built to manage your entire front-end toolchain, Node.js version, and package manager.  

This live demo will take you from start to finish, showing you a real migration. You'll leave knowing what Vite+ replaces today, what's coming next, and why a universal toolchain is a force multiplier when agents are writing and shipping code.

title: Treat your AI context as infrastructure

speakers.name: Christopher Harrison
speakers.title: Senior Developer Advocate
speakers.bio: Christopher is a longtime geek and developer at heart. He’s spent the better part of the last couple of decades enabling and upskilling developers on a variety of languages and platforms. He is currently at GitHub, focusing on helping organizations improve their DevX. When he’s not in front of a monitor, he can be found running many miles or spending time with his partner and their adopted fur baby.

abstract:
The best way to get Copilot to write the code you want is to give it the right context. Today that means some combination of custom agents, agent skills, instructions files, MCP servers, extensions, and plugins... and the list keeps growing.

So how do you choose the right tool for the right job and get those tools into your team's hands consistently? The answer is to treat your AI context as infrastructure. This session offers practical guidance for doing exactly that: what each of these building blocks is best at, how to decide between them, and how to standardize and distribute context across your organization so every developer benefits.

You'll leave able to map the current landscape of Copilot context tools to real use cases and with a strategy for managing that context as it grows.

title: How we optimize GitHub Copilot for every new model.

speakers.title: Product Manager
speakers.bio: Julie is a Product Manager working on Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot, focused on helping developers build with confidence and joy. She has always loved the editor space because it's where small ideas turn into reality: every day, millions of developers open VS Code to explore ideas, debug problems, and ship software. Today, her work centers on LLM releases in VS Code and Copilot Chat, bringing AI capabilities to developers in a practical, high-quality way and improving how they use AI in their daily workflows. She also focuses on offline evaluations for VS Code, building evals to measur

abstract: How do you ship a coding agent that works brilliantly across OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and whatever model drops next week? You build a harness. This session shares the evaluation framework the GitHub Copilot team uses to continuously test, measure, and optimize its coding agent across a matrix of clients, models, and configurations. You'll learn how the team defines reproducible benchmarks, the processes for running thousands of autonomous coding tasks, how LLM-graded assertions help catch regressions before users do, and the evaluation criteria for model integrations.

title: Sketching with code in the age of AI

speakers.title: CVP Engineering, GitHub Design and Microsoft CoreAI Design
speakers.bio: John is an American technologist and design leader who has spent his career translating between the worlds of computation, design, and business. It's a bridging act Wired once summed up this way: "Maeda is to design what Warren Buffett is to finance." He currently leads design across GitHub and Microsoft CoreAI as Corporate Vice President of Engineering, and serves on the board of directors of MillerKnoll. His path there runs through the MIT Media Lab, the presidency of the Rhode Island School of Design, a design partner role at Kleiner Perkins, and executive roles at Automattic, Publicis Sapi

abstract:
AI tools can now generate clean, functional output from a short prompt. The question is no longer how to write code, but how to understand what's been made.

Qianqian Ye shows why sketching and thinking in code, beyond syntax, is essential for working with AI. Drawing from teaching creative coding at USC and leading the open source creative coding tool p5.js (built on GitHub), Qianqian demonstrates how creative coding builds the intuition to shape systems (not just prompt them) and what's lost when that iterative process disappears.

John Maeda connects the dots between design, computation, and the creative judgment that AI can't replace. You'll leave with practical approaches for integrating AI into your workflow while keeping exploration and understanding intact.

title: Jev: Shipping a category-creator

speakers.name: Allie Laabs
speakers.title: Developer Relations
speakers.bio: Allie Laabs is a builder at heart who loves creating new things and turning them into memorable experiences. Her career spans software engineering, community management, and product management. These disciplines come together at TypeSafe, where she leads Developer Relations for Jev, the first public System One model. Her work includes building dozens of demos, including one that plays Doom, shaping documentation, and showing developers software they may not have imagined yet. Away from the keyboard, Allie is a professional burlesque and drag show producer and MC.

abstract: Every new primitive faces a similar launch problem. Docker and Lambda seem obvious now, but at launch developers had to be convinced they were worth learning. Jev, the first public System One model, faces that problem twice over: it asks developers to think harder about their code just as coding agents encourage them think about it less. Allie Laabs, lead DevRel at TypeSafe, shares how Jev was shipped: the two kinds of use cases developers needed to see, the small decisions that made the idea click, and the Doom demo that showed what intelligence inside the software loop looks like.

title: Prioritization as code: Assumptions by pull request, scored by AI

speakers.name: Mina Tawadrous
speakers.title: Associate Director, Product Management
speakers.bio: Mina leads Product in Platform Engineering at SiriusXM, where he works on developer productivity and experience, and on moving product decisions out of spreadsheets and into code. Before product management, he built games — a background that’s made him allergic to internal tools nobody wants to open. He’s previously spoken on “Assumptions as Code” and on how internal product management differs from its external counterpart. Across both, he’s made a habit of applying engineering rigor to the parts of product work that usually escape it. Based in Toronto, Mina is raising three kids, working thro

abstract:
Most product prioritization lives in spreadsheets and slide decks — far from the code and the engineers doing the work. One team solved this by moving prioritization into GitHub, the tool engineers already trust.  

Rubrics, assumptions, OKRs, and every scored initiative live in Markdown, with every decision shipped through a pull request. An AI agent drafts the scores, but humans own the judgment. When an assumption changes, a GitHub Action automatically re-scores every dependent initiative.  

This session demonstrates why having a single source of truth is so important. You’ll see what they built, learn how to adopt the same pattern, and understand why pull request reviews proved to be a more effective forum for prioritization than any meeting.
